name: Sindoor and kumkuma

card.summary: Red-orange powder worn at the hair parting or forehead in South Asian traditions as a cosmetic and cultural mark.
card.note: Some commercial powders have been found to contain lead.

quick.overview:
Sindoor is a vermilion-red to orange-red powder worn by married Hindu women along the hair parting (the maang), a visible marker of marital status and auspiciousness [1]. Kumkum is a related red powder, used especially in South India [1].

It works as a colour accent on the hairline and forehead. Traditional versions use turmeric with slaked lime; historic ones used cinnabar, and some modern products have used red lead or synthetic dyes [1].
quick.how: Brides receive it in a wedding ritual and then apply it daily, filling the parting or placing a small spot at the hairline or forehead [1].
quick.risks: Studies found lead in many commercial sindoor samples and linked it to childhood lead poisoning; a 2008 FDA testing led to recalls, and contact dermatitis from local cosmetics is also reported [1][2][3][4].

lead: Sindoor is a vermilion, orange-red or maroon cosmetic powder from South Asia, worn most commonly by married Hindu women at the hair parting; it signifies marital status, auspiciousness and fidelity [1]. Kumkum, associated more with South India, is a related red powder applied as a mark [1].

As a cosmetic it adds a strong red line or dot to the hair and forehead, and styles vary: new brides fill the parting, other married women may wear a spot at the hairline or forehead, and some younger women wear a triangular design [1].

Traditional sindoor mixes turmeric with slaked lime and alum, which reacts to form red; cinnabar-based vermilion (mercury sulfide) and, in modern commercial products, red lead or azo dyes have also been used [1]. Public health studies have examined lead content [2][3].

angle.text: Sindoor and kumkuma add a bold red accent to the hairline and forehead as part of traditional South Asian styling and as a cultural marker.

paras: Sindoor signals marital status; it is first applied in the Sindoor Daan wedding ritual by the husband and later applied by the wife daily, and widows typically stop wearing it [1]. Wikipedia notes the Vedas do not mention it and that its first verifiable scriptural reference is the Brahmanda Purana [1].

Historic vermilion was cinnabar, a mercury compound, and modern commercial products have contained red lead [1]. A study that bought 95 sindoor samples in New Jersey stores and 23 in India found lead in 83.2% of the US samples and 78.3% of the Indian ones [3]. Pediatric case reports describe lead poisoning in children exposed to imported cultural powders [2], and a case report links elevated family blood lead to sindoor used as food coloring [5]. Lead nephropathy due to sindoor has also been reported [6]. Wikipedia reports that in 2008 FDA testing found excess lead in imported sindoor, leading to recalls [1]. A study evaluated field tools for detecting lead in these powders [7], and a dermatology study from northern India covers contact dermatitis from local cosmetics [8].
Studies are of safety and contamination rather than of cosmetic benefit: lead content surveys, case reports and field testing methods [3][2][5][6][7].

timeline.event: US FDA testing finds high lead in imported sindoor, prompting recalls. [1]
